audit_metadata.page_or_scope: PyArcana S44 — CI/CD y seguridad de la cadena de suministro — append-only continuation after S44.patch-01.json
audit_metadata.audience_assumption: Learner has completed PyArcana through S43 but must not supply undocumented CI/CD or supply-chain knowledge.

major_comprehension_problems: The section repeatedly collapses policy scope into boolean/string predicates, causing the learner model to diverge from the real CI/CD control.
Uncertainty is routed before already observable breaches in multiple E3 classifiers, so a missing field can downgrade a known failure into a review state.
The section still contains learner-visible decorative or unexplained green signals that are not derived from evidence.
The opening SBOM explanation overstates scope and blurs SBOM component inventory with broader build inputs/provenance.
recurring_missing_context: permission scope: workflow-level default vs job-level exception
precedence when a record contains both missing evidence and an independently observable breach
terminology_inconsistencies: `write` is correctly presented in theory as sometimes necessary at job scope, but exercises treat every write value as a breach.
`conventional` appears as a boolean/status without a defined concept or relationship to the release gate.
recommended_global_rules: Model GitHub Actions permissions with explicit scope and required capability; never reduce least privilege to 'no write anywhere'.
Classify known breaches independently from missing evidence; a missing field must not erase a failure already proven by present fields.
Every printed green status must be computed from taught inputs or removed.
Define SBOM as an inventory of software components/dependencies and their relationships, with explicit scope/known unknowns; use provenance for build origin/process evidence.

terminology_registry.plain_language_meaning: GitHub Actions permission that allows the job's GITHUB_TOKEN to upload/publish packages; it can be legitimate when narrowly scoped to the job that needs it.
terminology_registry.recommended_first_introduction: En el workflow mantenemos permisos de solo lectura por defecto. El job que publica un paquete puede recibir `packages: write` solo durante ese job, porque necesita escribir en GitHub Packages; los demás permisos siguen en `none` o `read`.

terminology_registry.plain_language_meaning: Unknown in current S44. It may intend Conventional Commits, but the source never says so.
terminology_registry.recommended_first_introduction: Remove the signal unless the lesson explicitly intends to teach Conventional Commits; if retained, name and define the convention and derive the result from a commit message check.
terminology_registry.recommended_short_form_after_introductio: Only after source intent is confirmed.

terminology_registry.plain_language_meaning: Software Bill of Materials: a machine-readable inventory of software components/dependencies, information about them and their relationships.
terminology_registry.recommended_first_introduction: Una Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) es un inventario legible por máquinas de los componentes y dependencias de software incluidos en un producto, junto con información y relaciones entre esos componentes.

elements.current_content: The preamble calls a release job with `packages: write` a breach, and the solution requires every permission value to be in {read, none}.
elements.intended_function: Teach least privilege, immutable action pinning, secret scanning and dependency review.
elements.intended_audience: Advanced PyArcana learner practicing GitHub Actions hardening.

issues.problem: Theory correctly allows narrowly scoped job-level write permission when a release operation needs it, while E2/E3 rejects any `write` regardless of scope or capability.
issues.reader_question_created: Is every write permission insecure, or is a narrowly scoped release-job permission valid?
issues.recommended_fix: Represent workflow permissions and job permissions separately, and validate the minimum capability required by each job.

missing_context: Whether token_permissions represents workflow-level defaults or a specific job.
Which write capability the release job actually needs.
ambiguities: The word `write` is treated as a single risk category although GitHub permissions are capability-specific and scope-specific.
assumed_background_knowledge: GitHub Actions workflow-level vs job-level `permissions` resolution.
why_this_is_a_problem: A learner can form the false rule 'least privilege means no write permissions anywhere'.
That rule conflicts with publishing packages or creating attestations, where a narrowly scoped job legitimately needs write capability.
recommended_strategy: Allow only the exact write capability needed by the release/attestation job.
Use a broad unrelated write permission as the adversarial fixture instead.
elements.improved_content: En el workflow, los permisos por defecto se mantienen en `read`/`none`. Un job de publicación puede usar `packages: write` únicamente si ese job publica en GitHub Packages; ese permiso no debe heredarse por jobs que no lo necesitan. El ejercicio debe comprobar el alcance y la capacidad concreta, no rechazar cualquier valor `write`.

attack_defense_verdict.attack: Executed the canonical assessor against a release-job fixture with contents:read, packages:write, a full 40-hex SHA, zero secret hits and dependency_review=True.
attack_defense_verdict.defense: The exercise could have intended token_permissions to mean workflow-level defaults.
attack_defense_verdict.why_defense_fails: The learner-facing preamble explicitly says 'un job de release' and the data model contains no scope field, while S44 theory separately says a release job may receive narrowly scoped write permission.

notes: Proposed repair aligns the exercise with GitHub's workflow/job permission model.

elements.current_content: The learner is asked to predict `conventional True`; the code prints the value as a hard-coded constant and the surrounding explanation never defines `conventional` or uses it in release_ready().
elements.intended_function: Model branch/review policy and actionable release notes.

issues.problem: The term/status is undefined, not derived from any input and not part of the stated release contract.
issues.reader_question_created: What is conventional here—Conventional Commits, a release-note format, or something else—and why is it automatically true?
issues.recommended_fix: Remove the signal; or, if Conventional Commits is intended, define it and compute the result from a real commit-message fixture.

missing_context: Why it matters to the gate
ambiguities: Could refer to Conventional Commits, but that is not stated.
why_this_is_a_problem: The preamble explicitly asks the learner to attend to and predict a green status that contains no taught mechanism.
A hard-coded True makes the demonstration look like evidence even though no check occurred.
recommended_strategy: Remove the line as the minimum repair unless source intent confirms a real Conventional Commits objective.
elements.improved_content: Remove `conventional True` from this demo. Keep the observable outputs `reviews 2` and `release_notes True`, both of which are derived from the taught contract.
source_validation_questions: Did the author intend `conventional` to mean Conventional Commits? If yes, where is that concept supposed to be introduced and assessed?

attack_defense_verdict.attack: Searched current S44 for `conventional`; the only learner-facing occurrence is this hard-coded prediction/output pair.
attack_defense_verdict.defense: It may be a harmless mnemonic for a commit convention.
attack_defense_verdict.why_defense_fails: A harmless mnemonic should not be presented as a predicted green result without definition or input. Removing it costs nothing and reduces an unexplained signal.

notes: If the term is intentionally retained, source intent must be verified first.

elements.current_content: The SBOM is described as 'el inventario de todo lo que entró en tu artefacto'.
elements.intended_function: Give a beginner-accessible mental model of an SBOM before supply-chain controls.

issues.text: todo lo que entró en tu artefacto
issues.problem: The food-label analogy is useful, but 'everything' overstates SBOM scope. An SBOM inventories software components/dependencies and related information; broader build inputs and builder/workflow evidence belong to provenance or other evidence.
issues.reader_question_created: Should the SBOM contain every build script, compiler setting, workflow input and runner detail?
issues.recommended_fix: Keep the ingredients analogy but say 'componentes y dependencias de software' and state that provenance records how/by whom the artifact was built.

ambiguities: 'Todo' can be read literally as every build input.
why_this_is_a_problem: The learner can build a false mental model in which SBOM and provenance overlap completely.
Later evidence tasks depend on distinguishing component inventory from build provenance.
recommended_strategy: Preserve the nutrition-label analogy, narrow the noun phrase, immediately contrast it with provenance.
elements.improved_content: Piensa en la **Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)** como una etiqueta de ingredientes del software: enumera los componentes y dependencias de software incluidos en el artefacto, junto con información y relaciones entre ellos. Su alcance debe quedar claro; no sustituye la **provenance**, que registra evidencia sobre cómo y desde qué proceso se construyó el artefacto.

attack_defense_verdict.attack: Compared the literal 'todo' claim with CISA/NTIA definitions of SBOM as an inventory of software components/dependencies and their relationships.
attack_defense_verdict.defense: The ingredients-list analogy is common and pedagogically useful.
attack_defense_verdict.why_defense_fails: The analogy can be retained; only the absolute word 'todo' needs repair. The defect is overclaim, not the analogy.

notes: Definition matches current CISA/NTIA framing and keeps the original analogy.

elements.locator: T1-A-E3 and T2-A-E3 representative counterexamples; same missing-first pattern recurs across E3 tasks
elements.current_content: E3 functions return a review/inspection state immediately when any required field is missing, before checking other present fields for an independently observable breach.
elements.intended_function: Teach fail-closed handling of valid, breached and uncertain cases.

issues.text: if missing: return REVIEW_* before breach evaluation
issues.problem: Missing evidence is allowed to mask a known breach in another field. The classifier collapses two simultaneous facts into a weaker uncertainty state.
issues.reader_question_created: If a record is both incomplete and already demonstrably unsafe, should the pipeline merely request review or block for the known failure?
issues.recommended_fix: Evaluate independently observable breaches first (or collect both breach and missing reasons), then route pure uncertainty only when no known breach exists.

missing_context: Decision precedence for simultaneous breach + missing evidence
ambiguities: The prose defines breach and uncertainty separately but never explains mixed-state precedence.
why_this_is_a_problem: T1-A counterexample: lint=False with supported missing returns REVIEW_MATRIX instead of FAIL_CI_GATE.
T2-A counterexample: write permission + @v4 + secret_hits=1 with dependency_review missing returns SECURITY_APPROVAL instead of the breach path.
A learner can infer that deleting a field weakens a known failure into an uncertainty/review state.
recommended_strategy: Compute all violations that can be decided from present fields.
If any known breach exists, block with the breach decision and retain missing-field metadata.
Only use REVIEW/INSPECT/APPROVAL when the record is incomplete and no known breach is already observable.
elements.improved_content: Clasifica dos dimensiones por separado: **breaches observables** y **evidencia faltante**. Si ya existe un breach comprobable, el pipeline bloquea aunque también falten campos; la ausencia se conserva como información adicional. Solo usa `REVIEW_*` cuando no hay un breach demostrado y la falta de evidencia impide decidir.

attack_defense_verdict.attack: Executed mixed-state mutations against canonical T1-A-E3 and T2-A-E3 classifiers.
attack_defense_verdict.defense: Schema validation first avoids KeyError and makes missing data explicit.
attack_defense_verdict.why_defense_fails: Safe access does not require suppressing known breaches. The evaluator can inspect present fields first/independently and still report missing schema.

notes: Repair preserves human review for genuine uncertainty while making mixed states fail closed.

cross_element_issues.issue: T2-A theory and T2-A We Do encode incompatible least-privilege rules.
cross_element_issues.recommended_fix: Use scope-aware workflow/job permission fixtures across all three surfaces.

cross_element_issues.issue: The E3 exercise family confuses pure uncertainty with mixed uncertainty+breach.
cross_element_issues.recommended_fix: Adopt one explicit precedence rule and retain multiple reasons instead of single mutually exclusive labels.

cross_element_issues.issue: Current canonical source has estimatedHours=9 while the public rendered snapshot observed during the audit reports 20h.
cross_element_issues.recommended_fix: Resolve the deployed SHA/build source before changing either value; do not guess which number is authoritative.

summary.most_important_global_improvement: Make decisions depend on authentic evidence with explicit scope and preserve all simultaneously known failure reasons.

Why does public S44 currently show 20h while canonical source says 9h?

finding_delta.title: Least-privilege exercise rejects legitimate scoped job-level write permissions.
`conventional True` is an unexplained, hard-coded green signal.
Opening SBOM mental model overstates scope as everything that entered the artifact.
Missing-first E3 routing masks independently observable breaches.

fixer_invariants: Least privilege is scoped minimum authority, not a blanket ban on every write permission.
A missing field cannot erase a breach already proven by fields that are present.
A printed green status must be derived from taught evidence, not a literal True.
SBOM inventories software components/dependencies; provenance covers build origin/process evidence.
